Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The characteristic equation of a square matrix [MATH: A] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \det(A-\lambda I)=0.]

Content:
On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I),] which we call the characteristic polynomial of the matrix [MATH: A.]

Content:
For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix [MATH: [− 8|− 9; 6|7]]
[MATH: p(λ)|= det(C − λI); = − 8 − λ|− 9; 6|7 − λ; = (− 8 − λ) ⋅ (7 − λ) − (− 9) ⋅ 6; = λ^{2} + λ − 2]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices

Content:
What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [a|b; c|d]]

Content:
First, let's find the characteristic equation:
[MATH: det(A − λI)|= 0; a − λ|b; c|d − λ|= 0; (a − λ)(d − λ) − bc|= 0; λ^{2} − (a + d)λ + (ad − bc)|= 0]

Content:
Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix:

Content:
[MATH: \det(A) = ad-bc]

Content:
The coefficient of [MATH: \lambda] is the sum of the diagonal entries of [MATH: A] taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix [MATH: A] is called the trace of [MATH: A,] and we denote it as

Content:
[MATH: \mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.]

Content:
So, for any [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: A], the characteristic polynomial is

Content:
[MATH: p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).]

Content:
Note: This result can be extended to the general case of [MATH: n \times n] matrices. If [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

Content:
[MATH: p(λ)|= det(A − λI); = (− 1)^{n}λ^{n} + c_{n − 1}λ^{n − 1} + ⋯ + c_{1}λ + c_{0}; = (− 1)^{n}λ^{n} + (− 1)^{n − 1}tr(A)_(⏟)_(c_{n − 1})λ^{n − 1} + ⋯ + c_{1}λ + det(A)_(⏟)_(c_{0}),]
where

Content:
[MATH: c_{n − 1} = (− 1)^{n − 1}tr(A)andc_{0} = det(A).]

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: [9|1; 2|− 6]] find the sum of the eigenvalues of [MATH: A.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The characteristic polynomial of [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: p(λ)|= λ^{2} − tr(A)λ + det(A).]

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of [MATH: p(\lambda),] i.e., the eigenvalues of [MATH: A,] satisfy

[MATH: {λ_{1} + λ_{2} = tr(A); λ_{1} ⋅ λ_{2} = det(A).]

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of [MATH: A] is equal to the trace of [MATH: A.]

Therefore,
[MATH: \lambda_1+\lambda_2 = \textrm{tr}(A)= 9+(-6)=3.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem

Content:
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states the following:

Content:
> Let [MATH: A] be an [MATH: \,n \!\times\! n] matrix whose characteristic polynomial is
> [MATH: p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.]
> Then, the matrix [MATH: A] is a solution of the characteristic equation [MATH: p(\lambda) = 0].

Content:
That is to say, if we substitute [MATH: A] into the characteristic polynomial [MATH: p(\lambda)], taking [MATH: A^0 = I,] then we have
[MATH: p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,]

Content:
where [MATH: O] is the zero-matrix.

Content:
For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix
[MATH: [− 8|− 9; 6|7]]
whose characteristic polynomial is
[MATH: p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,]
we have
[MATH: p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The characteristic polynomial of [MATH: A] is given by

[MATH: p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A).]

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

[MATH: p(A)|= O; A^{2} − tr(A)A + det(A)I|= O; A^{2}|= tr(A)A − det(A)I; A^{2}|= − 4A + 18I.]

Therefore, [MATH: x+y = -4+18 = 14.]
